Promt 1: 
I have uploaded a set of documents (mostly research papers) about steelmaking,  
energy efficiency, and intelligent automation / furnace scheduling. 
 
For EVERY uploaded document, extract the following metadata and present it as  
a table with one row per document: 
 
| # | File name | Title | Authors | Journal / Source | Publication date | Keywords | Snippet | 
 
Rules: 
- Use only information that is actually in the documents. If a field is  
  missing, write "not stated". Do not guess or invent anything. 
- Keywords: use the author keywords if listed; otherwise write "not stated". 
- Snippet: the first 1–2 sentences of the abstract (or the introduction if  
  there is no abstract). 
- After the table, tell me how many documents you processed, and list any  
  files you could not read. 
 
Output the table so I can copy it into Excel. 
 
Promt2: 
Based on the inventory table above, write a short "Initial Scan" section  
(about 300–400 words) for a university assignment. It should: 
 
1. Define the boundaries of the knowledge domain: which main topics the  
   documents cover (group them into 3–6 thematic clusters), and what is  
   clearly outside the scope. 
2. Acknowledge the complexity of the problem: why reducing operational  
   complexity, improving energy efficiency, and automating furnace  
   scheduling in steelmaking is difficult, and why the knowledge in the  
   document set is currently fragmented.

   (e.g. GenAI-based metadata extraction with Microsoft 365 Copilot,  
   thematic clustering by keywords, and later synthesis steps).

Write in clear academic English.

Processing summary 
Documents processed: 31 of 31. Files that could not be read: none. 
Notes on data quality: 
• #11 (Neuer et al.): the PDF text layer scrambles the author block; the seven names are certain, but the order shown may differ from the printed order (marked *). 
• #9 (Shah et al.): article in press without volume or publication date; only the acceptance date is given. 
• #4, #13, #19: only the year is stated; no exact publication date appears in the documents. 
• #14, #16, #25: no publication date printed; the acceptance date and the year from the citation line are shown. 

Page 9 
• #15 (Rao & Zhang): no author keywords. 
• #5, #10, #12, #28 (IEEE): keywords are taken from “Index Terms”, IEEE’s equivalent of author keywords. 
 
 
 
Initial Scan 
The document set (n = 31) spans roughly 2016–2026 and defines a knowledge domain at the intersection of production scheduling, energy management and intelligent automation in steelmaking. Keyword-based grouping yields five 
thematic clusters: 
1. Furnace and heat-treatment scheduling, the largest cluster. It includes idle-energy minimisation (Benedikt et al., 2021), reheating-furnace scheduling (Xu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026) and heat-treatment batching (Wang et al., 
2016; Gomes et al., 2021). 
2. Scheduling across steelmaking, casting and rolling under uncertainty, covering machine breakdowns, release-time variability and robust hot-strip-mill planning (Wang et al., 2019; Long et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023). 
3. Plant-level energy systems and demand response, including by-product gas networks and electricity-market participation (Pena et al., 2019; Shah et al., in press). 
4. Data-driven automation, namely deep reinforcement learning and digital twins (Wang et al., 2025; Müller-Zhang et al., 2023). 
5. Human-centred and explainable AI, spanning XAI for scheduling algorithms and human-in-the-loop design (Morandini et al., 2023; Mehdiyev et al., 2024; Arunthavanathan et al., 2024). 
Several topics lie clearly outside the scope. These include metallurgical and material-science questions, combustion and heat-transfer modelling, low-carbon process routes such as hydrogen-based steelmaking, and economic or policy 
analyses. 
The problem is complex for several reasons. Steel production is a multi-stage, tightly coupled process, so a decision at one stage, such as a slab's charging time, propagates to downstream operations (Li et al., 2026). Scheduling problems 
in this setting are typically NP-hard and nonconvex. They are further complicated by uncertain processing times, energy prices and material supply, and by the trade-off between energy use and productivity (Gomes et al., 2021). 
Automation adds a further tension: high-performing methods such as deep reinforcement learning are opaque, which undermines operator trust (Theumer et al., 2022). 
The knowledge in the set is currently fragmented. Most studies optimise a single process stage using a problem-specific model, and methods, objectives and data bases differ widely. Explainability research is largely tested on generic job 
shops rather than on steel processes, while steel-specific studies rarely address transparency or the human role.

I selected three sub-topics that show genuine methodological tension rather than consensus:

Step 2A — Modeling Uncertainty in Scheduling 
Documents: #2 (Wang, Liu & Jin, 2019), #3 (Long et al., 2020), #7 (Wang et al., 2016), #28 (Zhang, Song & Wu, 2023) 
Three distinct philosophies appear. Wang et al. (2016, #7) use fuzzy logic, representing gas heating values, processing times, and due dates as triangular fuzzy numbers and resolving dominance via a centroid-distance ranking. This avoids 
requiring probability distributions but depends on subjectively chosen fuzzy-spread parameters; the paper itself shows that a narrower fuzzy spread yields better objective values, i.e., the method's performance depends on how much 
uncertainty is assumed. 
Wang, Liu & Jin (2019, #2) and Long et al. (2020, #3) instead use stochastic, simulation-based approaches: the former builds a surrogate (SVR) model to approximate machine-breakdown scenarios, while the latter forecasts release times 
and embeds forecast error into a chance-constrained model solved via Monte Carlo simulation. Both require historical data and computationally expensive scenario evaluation. 
Zhang, Song & Wu (2023, #28), by contrast, apply robust optimization, which does not require a probability distribution at all — instead it guarantees feasibility across a bounded uncertainty set, at the cost of potentially conservative 
(less efficient) schedules, per the standard robust-optimization critique reflected in the abstract's framing. 
Trade-off for the organization: Fuzzy and robust methods reduce data requirements but risk conservatism or subjectivity; stochastic/surrogate methods can be more accurate but demand historical data and heavier computation. The 
organization must decide whether it has enough reliable historical data to justify a stochastic approach, or whether a simpler, more conservative fuzzy/robust model is preferable where data is scarce. 
 
Step 2B — Modeling Furnace Idle-Time and Energy Behaviour 
Documents: #1 (Benedikt et al., 2021), #31 (Hidri et al., 2021), #14 (Duan et al., 2025) 
Benedikt et al. (#1) argue explicitly, in their own literature comparison, that the common industry practice of modeling machine behaviour with a small set of discrete modes (e.g., "on," "off," "stand-by," connected by a static transition 
graph) is too restrictive. They instead model the furnace's full continuous-time dynamics via a bilinear differential equation and derive a continuous, concave "idle energy function," showing (via their own numerical experiments) that this 
achieves markedly lower average power per idle period than the mode-based approach.

Contrast: #1 optimizes within idle periods using a physically detailed model; #31 avoids the idle-period problem by structurally removing idle time; #14 does not schedule at all but supports decision-making through prediction. These are

Trade-off for the organization: A continuous-dynamics approach like #1 requires furnace-specific system identification (as demonstrated with the Škoda Auto case) and is not readily transferable; the no-idle constraint (#31) is simpler to 
implement but presumes idle time can always be avoided, which may not hold for furnace-based (thermal-inertia) equipment. The organization must choose between investing in furnace-specific physical modeling for larger energy 
savings, or adopting a simpler structural constraint that is easier to generalize but may be infeasible for slow-dynamics equipment like furnaces. 
 
Step 2C — Choice of Optimization Method: Online Speed vs. Solution Optimality

Wang et al. (#5) and Shah et al. (#9) both use deep reinforcement learning explicitly because it allows scheduling decisions to be made via a fast function evaluation rather than solving a large optimization model online. Shah et al. state
